cards.title: Does UEOPL equal EOPL?
cards.formal: Does EndOfPotentialLine reduce to UniqueEOPL by a deterministic polynomial-time many-one reduction for total search problems? Equivalently, is UEOPL=EOPL? Instances contain explicit Boolean circuits, and the reduction may inspect their descriptions. The question concerns the ordinary classes without an oracle.
cards.why: Would determine whether uniqueness with efficiently detectable violations defines a strictly easier form of total search inside PLS∩PPAD, affecting the classification of fixed-point, orientation and game problems captured by UEOPL.
cards.status_note: Checked the canonical definitions, the 2022 collapse, and the published 2024 separation. Searches through 12 September 2026, including the abstracts of Super Unique Tarski is in UEOPL and On Cutting Cakes and Crossing Curves, found no resolution of the ordinary class equality. Those later applications are not equality or separation results.

progress.text: The defining paper proves UEOPL⊆EOPL and conjectures strict containment.

cards.definitions: A total NP search problem is a polynomial-time decidable relation R(a,z) with polynomially bounded witnesses z and at least one witness for every input a. A reduction R≤S consists of deterministic polynomial-time maps F and G such that every S-witness w for F(a) gives an R-witness G(a,w); running times are polynomial in the explicit input lengths. For EndOfPotentialLine, an instance consists of circuits P,S:{0,1}ⁿ→{0,1}ⁿ and V:{0,1}ⁿ→{0,…,2ᵐ−1}, for n,m≥1, with P(0ⁿ)=0ⁿ, S(0ⁿ)≠0ⁿ and V(0ⁿ)=0. Potentials are m-bit nonnegative integers. A valid answer is a vertex x satisfying at least one of: (a) P(S(x))≠x; (b) x≠0ⁿ and S(P(x))≠x; (c) x≠S(x), P(S(x))=x and V(S(x))≤V(x). UniqueEOPL has the same instances and accepts all these answers, and additionally accepts two vertices x≠y with x≠S(x), y≠S(y), and either V(x)=V(y) or V(x)<V(y)<V(S(x)). Thus uniqueness is enforced by additional verifiable witnesses, not assumed as an unverifiable promise. Circuits are finite acyclic AND/OR/NOT circuits with their complete gate lists as input; size includes all gates, wires, input and output labels. The displayed restrictions at 0ⁿ are directly checkable; malformed encodings or failed restrictions may be assigned a distinguished trivial answer. EOPL and UEOPL consist of all total NP search problems reducible to their respective canonical problems by the reductions just defined. In particular UEOPL⊆EOPL, since an EndOfPotentialLine answer is always also a UniqueEOPL answer.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove equality by a polynomial-time reduction from EndOfPotentialLine to UniqueEOPL, valid for every output that the target relation permits, or prove that no such reduction exists. A separation limited to oracle queries or decision trees does not establish inequality of the ordinary circuit-defined classes.

cards.title: NP-completeness of conditional time-bounded Kolmogorov complexity for Turing-machine programs
cards.formal: Do there exist fixed polynomials t and ζ for which the standard Turing-machine version of McKᵗP[ζ] is NP-complete under randomized polynomial-time many-one reductions? Its instances are an output string x, an auxiliary string z of length ζ(|x|), and a program-length threshold k; the question is whether some program of at most k bits outputs x from z within t(|x|) steps. The source proves the RAM-program version and explicitly leaves the Turing-machine version open. The precise reference-machine convention still needs specification.
cards.why: Would determine whether a natural NP-completeness result about bounded description length extends beyond random-access programs, clarifying how machine conventions affect the connection between compression, meta-complexity and cryptography.
cards.status_note: Read the original definitions and theorem, and the March 2026 full chain-rule revision corresponding to STOC 2026. Searches through 12 September 2026 found no theorem settling the exact standard-TM question. The formal reference-machine convention remains to be fixed.

progress.text: Theorem 1.2 proves the RAM-program result under randomized reductions and explicitly leaves the TM-program version open.

cards.definitions: For a specified deterministic universal interpreter U, let Kᵗ_U(x|z)=min{|p|:U(p,z) halts with output exactly x within t(|x|) steps}, with value +∞ when there is no such program. Programs p and strings x,z are binary; the auxiliary string is given as input without being included in |p|. The intended alternative to the paper’s RAM model uses sequential Turing-machine access to z, rather than unit-cost access to an arbitrary indexed bit. For fixed integer-valued polynomials t,ζ on nonnegative integers, define L_{U,t,ζ} to contain triples (x,z,k) with n=|x|≥2, |z|=ζ(n), k a binary integer encoded in exactly ⌈log₂ n⌉ bits, and Kᵗ_U(x|z)≤k. Ill-formed triples are rejected. These length and threshold conventions follow McKᵗP[ζ] in the source; finitely many shorter x can be treated separately. Input size counts x,z and k in full, and t,ζ are fixed functions, not part of an instance. A randomized many-one reduction from a language A to L is a polynomial-time randomized map R with Pr[R(a)∈L]≥2/3 for every a∈A and Pr[R(a)∉L]≥2/3 for every a∉A. NP-completeness here means L∈NP and such a reduction from every NP language, not deterministic Karp completeness. Under a fixed polynomial-time simulation convention, membership is verified by guessing a program and checking its bounded computation. The remaining convention is how U encodes and simulates TM programs and which computation’s steps define the exact budget.
cards.answer_criterion: After specifying the reference TM convention, prove the existence of fixed polynomial bounds t,ζ for which the stated exact decision language is NP-complete under randomized many-one reductions, or refute that existence claim. A RAM theorem, a SAT-oracle version, or hardness conditional on an additional cryptographic assumption does not by itself resolve the unconditional TM question. The source does not justify replacing this question by deterministic-reduction completeness or by its stronger for-every-t RAM theorem.

context_blocks.title: Short programs with side information
context_blocks.text: A program can use z to generate x, so the shortest description may be much smaller than x itself. The question asks about the computational difficulty of deciding whether such a short description exists under a polynomial time budget.

context_blocks.title: What the 2022 result establishes
context_blocks.text: For every polynomial t(n)≥n², the paper obtains some polynomial ζ for which its RAM-based language is NP-complete under randomized reductions. The auxiliary input can be substantially longer than the time bound, making its access model significant.

context_blocks.title: Machine simulation does not automatically transfer exact thresholds
context_blocks.text: Polynomial overhead in simulating one machine by another is enough for many complexity-class comparisons. Here the accepted programs are selected by simultaneous time and description-length limits; a transfer theorem must preserve the relevant yes/no instances. The source therefore states the TM case separately.

context_blocks.title: The 2026 chain-rule result addresses a different formulation
context_blocks.text: The later paper relates chain rules to the complexity of a promise problem separating short descriptions at time t from longer descriptions even at a polynomially enlarged time bound. Its NP-hardness discussion retains an extra hypothesis, and does not establish the unconditional exact TM completeness requested here.

context_blocks.title: Remaining formulation issue
context_blocks.text: The primary paper formally specifies its RAM model but refers to the alternative only as the standard Turing-machine version. To make this a single exact language, fix the sequential universal interpreter/program encoding and whether the time budget counts interpreter transitions or transitions of the encoded machine, or establish a precise model-invariance statement covering them. The card records the existential polynomial-bound question suggested before Theorem 1.2; it does not silently demand that the theorem hold for every t(n)≥n² in the TM model.

cards.title: A uniform exponent saving for arbitrary generalized convolution
cards.formal: Does there exist an absolute ε>0 such that, for every fixed finite domain D with d=|D|≥2 and every fixed function f:D×D→D, the entire f-convolution of two integer tables on Dⁿ can be computed exactly in Õ(d^{(2−ε)n}·polylog(2+M)) time? The same ε must work for all domains and operations; n is unbounded and M bounds the absolute input values. No associativity, commutativity or algebraic structure of f is assumed.
cards.why: Would give a broadly applicable improvement for table-merging computations without requiring an algebraic law on the state-combination operation, strengthening a common primitive in exact and parameterized algorithms.
cards.status_note: Read the IPEC question and the improved Algorithmica version, including its retained Section 6 question. Checked the January 2023 arXiv revision and later exact-title/generalized-convolution searches through 12 September 2026; no result meeting the uniform exponent target was found.

progress.text: The conference paper beats brute force by a factor (6/5)ⁿ for even d and asks for an absolute saving in the d-exponent.

cards.definitions: Identify D with {0,…,d−1}. For u,w∈Dⁿ set (u⊕_f w)ⱼ=f(uⱼ,wⱼ) for 1≤j≤n. Input tables g,h:Dⁿ→{−M,…,M}, with n≥1 and M≥1, list every signed integer in binary. The output is the full table C:Dⁿ→Z, where C(v)=Σ_{u,w∈Dⁿ: u⊕_f w=v}g(u)h(w); an empty sum is zero. All arithmetic is ordinary integer arithmetic. In the source’s fixed-operation convention, D and the finite d²-entry table of f specify the convolution problem; the growing inputs are g,h. More explicitly, the requested bound means a deterministic algorithm, uniform in n and the input tables, taking at most C_{D,f} d^{(2−ε)n}(1+n log d+log(2+M))^{a_{D,f}} bit operations, for constants C_{D,f},a_{D,f} depending only on D,f. Any finite preparation of that fixed table can be included in C_{D,f}; ε is chosen before D,f. This states the fixed-domain asymptotic question from the source, not a bound for reading an arbitrary operation table when n=1. Standard random-access storage of the listed tables is permitted, with arithmetic charged for operand bit length; addressing costs are absorbed in the displayed polynomial factor. Each output has O(n log d+log(2+M)) bits. The target concerns every output entry, not a query for a single specified v.
cards.answer_criterion: Establish the bound with one positive ε independent of D and f, for all fixed finite operations and all input tables, or refute that universally quantified existence claim in the stated deterministic exact-computation model. An exponent saving that tends to zero with d, a theorem restricted to selected operations, or a faster single-entry query algorithm does not suffice.

context_blocks.title: A common table-combination problem
context_blocks.text: Many exact algorithms combine two tables of partial solutions coordinate by coordinate. The function f specifies how one pair of coordinate states combines; the convolution sums the contributions of every compatible pair.

context_blocks.title: The input size and the brute-force cost differ
context_blocks.text: There are dⁿ entries in each input table and in the output, whereas there are d^{2n} pairs of input indices. The question asks for a fixed saving in this exponent for arbitrary coordinate-combination rules.

context_blocks.title: The full version improves the published conference bound
context_blocks.text: The journal theorem computes the full convolution in Õ(((3/4)d²)ⁿ polylog M) for even d; for odd d the base is (3/4)d²+(1/4)d. This improves the conference constant 5/6.

context_blocks.title: Why a smaller base does not settle this target
context_blocks.text: For even d the known bound corresponds to ε_d=log_d(4/3). It is positive for each fixed d but approaches zero as d grows. The open question requires a single positive ε valid for all d.

context_blocks.title: A single value is a different task
context_blocks.text: The paper also obtains Õ(d^{ωn/2} polylog M) for one requested output entry, where ω is the matrix-multiplication exponent. The card requires all dⁿ entries within the total time bound.

meta.status_scope: No claim of exhaustive open-status verification
methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. We aim for benchmarks of 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. All three use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The possible 1,000-problem expansion has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Deleted records are absent from the catalogue and exports. Their stable IDs and reasons are retained to prevent reimport. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The targets are 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. Top 100, Top 500 and the possible Top 1000 use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Records marked resolved are placed after the remaining candidates, without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.
